findings.title: Blocklist lookup is case-sensitive and does not trim
findings.body: BlockedEmail.should_block? loads a row with BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first, and the model never normalizes email before the uniqueness check or save. Signup stores the address exactly as submitted (User.new_from_params assigns params[:email] with no downcase or strip), and the new client cache compares that same raw string via rejectedEmails.contains. On PostgreSQL the unique index and equality match are case-sensitive, so a block row for bad@spam.com does not match Bad@spam.com, BAD@spam.com, or bad@spam.com with leading or trailing whitespace. Those are the same mailbox in practice (UsersController#change_email already does Email.downcase(...).strip), so a blocked address can still register by changing case or padding spaces, and after one rejection the signup form will allow that variant through again. Downcase and strip on write and inside should_block? before the query, and enforce case-insensitive uniqueness so mixed-case duplicates cannot be stored.

findings.title: should_block? writes during validation and double-counts
findings.body: should_block? is not a pure predicate: on every hit it does match_count += 1, sets last_match_at, and calls record.save, and EmailValidator calls it from User validation. UsersController#create always evaluates user.valid? and then user.save, and save runs validations again, so one signup attempt invokes should_block? twice. The first save commits immediately. The second runs inside the user-save transaction: if the user is persisted (including action_type do_nothing, which still updates stats), both increments commit and match_count rises by 2; if validation fails, the inner increment rolls back and the count rises by 1. Paths that only save once, such as User.create_for_email, rise by 1. Any valid? call, including a check that never creates a user, also mutates the row. The read-modify-write is racy under concurrent signups, and a failure in that save (lock timeout, StatementInvalid) escapes the validator and is rescued in create as login.something_already_taken. Record the match with one atomic UPDATE that does not run validations, and do not write from inside validation on every valid?/save pass.

findings.title: Domain allow/deny regex is unanchored and can be bypassed
findings.body: email_in_restriction_setting? builds Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true) after only escaping dots, then uses value =~ regexp, which succeeds on any substring. With email_domains_whitelist set to example.com, attacker@example.com.evil.com matches @example.com and is treated as allowed. Someone who controls that domain can receive the activation message and register even though the address is not on example.com. The same pattern does not cover subdomains on the blacklist: spam.com does not match user@mail.spam.com, so a subdomain of a blocked provider is accepted. Other metacharacters in the site setting are interpolated raw, so a value with an unmatched parenthesis makes Regexp.new raise and turns every email change into a 500. Compare normalized domains (anchor at the end of the address, or split the setting and test equality) instead of a substring regex.

findings.title: Email change never consults the blocklist
findings.body: The new block check only runs from EmailValidator when a User is validated with email_changed?. UsersController#change_email never assigns user.email or saves the user. It only rejects the address if User.where("email = ?", lower_email).exists?, then creates an EmailToken and enqueues an authorization mail to that address. A blocked address therefore passes this endpoint and a confirmation message is sent. Whether the address actually sticks depends on EmailToken.confirm later performing a validating save; this request path itself does not enforce BlockedEmail.should_block?, so the control added for signup is missing on the email-change flow. Reject blocked addresses here before creating the token, using the same normalization as lower_email.

findings.title: rejectedEmails array is shared across controller instances
findings.body: rejectedEmails: Em.A([]) is evaluated once when CreateAccountController is defined, so the array sits on the prototype. pushObject mutates that array in place rather than assigning a per-instance property. Every instance then shares one list: a second controller (tests, App.reset(), or another create()) already contains emails rejected elsewhere and will fail emailValidation for them via contains. Set a fresh array in init with this.set('rejectedEmails', Em.A()) so instances do not leak rejections into each other.

findings.title: Validator specs stub the block check and miss bypasses
findings.body: The EmailValidator examples stub BlockedEmail.should_block? and never insert a BlockedEmail, so they cannot catch a case or whitespace mismatch, a failed lookup, or the write inside should_block?. blocked_email_spec.rb only uses the exact address block@spamfromhome.org and calls should_block? once, so it stays green if Bad@spam.com or a trailing space is allowed, and if UsersController#create increments match_count twice. Domain whitelist and blacklist behavior was moved into EmailValidator with no regression example, including the unanchored match of attacker@example.com.evil.com against a whitelist of example.com. Add cases for normalized lookup, a single stat update on the signup path, and anchored domain restrictions.
